request: The ultimatum game: you get $100 to split with a stranger who can say no. How much would you offer? A two-voice dialogue. #interactive #short
subtitle: You have $100 to split with a stranger who can refuse. Make your offer, then hear what people really do and why low offers get turned down.

spec.title: You have $100 to split with a stranger. How much would you offer?

sources.title: An experimental analysis of ultimatum bargaining
sources.authors: W. Güth, R. Schmittberger, B. Schwarze
sources.finding: the first ultimatum game experiment: many proposers offered close to half, and low offers were rejected

sources.title: Behavioral Game Theory
sources.finding: across many studies, mean offers are about 40 % of the pie; offers below 20 % are rejected about half the time

sources.title: Dictator games: a meta study
sources.finding: when the receiver cannot refuse, dictators give on average about 28 %, and about two in three give something

commands.speak: Say I hand you a hundred dollars, but you must offer part of it to a stranger. How much would you give?
If they accept, you each keep your share. If they refuse, you both get nothing.

ask.question: How many of the 100 dollars would you offer the stranger? Click on the line.
ask.right: You offered {o}. In experiments, the typical offer is about forty.

commands.speak: Wait. Why not offer one dollar? One dollar beats nothing.
That's what the textbook says: a purely selfish stranger takes the dollar.
But real strangers don't. Offers under twenty dollars are turned down about half the time.
They'd rather walk away with nothing than take an insult?
Werner Güth and his colleagues first showed it in Germany in 1982, and it has been repeated around the world.
So offers cluster around forty to fifty: people offer what they expect to be accepted.
So my fairness is really fear of being turned down?
Partly. When the stranger cannot refuse at all, offers drop to about thirty, but most people still give something.
